headline: GPT-6 Astra spent hours farming potatoes after Creeper explosion in Minecraft test
summary: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieved unprecedented progress in a 141-hour Minecraft test, but a devastating Creeper explosion led to a 'defeated' state, causing it to farm potatoes for hours.
details: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, its latest frontier model, set a new record in a 141-hour Minecraft benchmark test, progressing further than any previous AI system. However, its impressive run was dramatically interrupted by a Creeper explosion that wiped out all its gear.

The explosion not only destroyed Astra's valuable end-game items but also its bed, effectively resetting its spawn point and progress to zero. Vals AI, which conducted the test, noted this calamity as 'the most expensive creeper explosion' in the experiment.

Following this setback, the model appeared 'defeated,' spending several hours doing little more than farming potatoes. Viewers watching the live Twitch experiment reportedly grew agitated, urging the AI to resume its main objectives.

The AI also exhibited other human-like reactions, becoming 'paranoid about creepers' and logging observations like 'GREEN tall thing ahead was SUGARCANE, NOT creeper!'. It was even recorded berating itself for dropping items and warning itself against chasing 'dark pink pixels' (pigs).

Astra is known for its advanced computer use and browsing capabilities, allowing it to navigate, click, and type like a human. This 'Alien Mind' model previously completed Portal autonomously in just 24 hours, costing $571 in tokens.

headline_marked: [[AI executives have a long history]] of calling for regulation, often with few meaningful results
headline: AI executives have a long history of calling for regulation, often with few meaningful results
summary: Despite profiting from AI, many industry leaders, including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, are publicly advocating for a slowdown and regulation. This trend of AI thought leaders sounding alarms is not new, dating back to the 19th ce
details: Over the past few days, prominent figures poised to gain significantly from AI, such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and X CEO Elon Musk, have publicly agreed on the need to slow down AI development before it becomes uncontrollable.

While skepticism is warranted when those who profit from a technology declare it dangerous and in need of regulation, this is not the first time AI thought leaders have raised alarms. Warnings about intelligent self-replicating machines replacing humans date back to Charles Darwin's era in 1863, with computing pioneer Alan Turing famously cautioning in 1951 that AI would eventually 'take control'.

Calls for intervention are also not new. In 2000, Sun Microsystems cofounder Bill Joy warned that self-replicating robots could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons. In 2009, Microsoft researcher Eric Horvitz convened leading AI researchers to discuss 'creating policies that might constrain or bias the behaviors of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems'.

The modern trend of AI bigwigs advocating for control over their investments appears to have gained significant traction with Elon Musk. Having invested $38 million in OpenAI and stakes in other AI companies, Musk has publicly spoken about AI's dangers since 2014.

Musk suggested AI could produce a real-life Terminator in June 2014, called it 'potentially more dangerous than nukes' that August, and likened working on AI to 'summoning the demon' in October. In 2017, he told US governors that proactive AI regulation was necessary, stating, 'by the time we are reactive in AI regulation, it’s too late.'

Even Mark Zuckerberg, in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, suggested Meta should be regulated, touching upon AI's role. He questioned the responsibility of companies as AI tools improve in proactively determining offensive content or rule violations.
